related_questions.question: What is the G-1145 application form?

text_blocks.snippet: Form G-1145, E-Notification of Application/Petition Acceptance, is a one-page form used to request electronic notification from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) when they accept your immigration application or petition. It allows you to receive email and/or text message updates on the status of your application, rather than relying solely on mail.
snippet_highlighted_words: a one-page form used to request electronic notification from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) when they accept your immigration application or petition

list.title: Purpose:
list.snippet: The primary purpose of Form G-1145 is to provide a faster and more convenient way for applicants to be notified about the acceptance of their immigration forms.

list.title: How it works:
list.snippet: You simply attach Form G-1145 to the front of your application or petition when submitting it to USCIS.

list.title: What you receive:
list.snippet: USCIS will send you an email and/or text message (depending on what you specify on the form) within 24 hours of accepting your application.

list.title: Benefits:
list.snippet: This electronic notification can be quicker than waiting for the traditional mail receipt, which can take up to 30 days according to New Frontier Immigration Law.

list.title: Where to file:
list.snippet: Form G-1145 is typically filed with applications that are submitted to a USCIS lockbox facility, such as family and marriage green card applications.
Form G-1145 is optional, but it's recommended for applications sent to lockboxes.
It's not needed for applications sent directly to a USCIS service center or field office.
You'll still receive the official receipt notice (Form I-797C) by mail even if you submit Form G-1145 according to Boston University.
The email and text message will only provide the receipt number and information on how to check your case status; it won't include any personal information.
A locked padlock or https:// is used to secure .gov websites.

related_questions.question: What medical conditions disqualify for a green card?

text_blocks.snippet: Certain medical conditions can make an individual inadmissible to the United States, potentially disqualifying them from obtaining a green card. These conditions generally fall into a few categories: communicable diseases of public health significance, mental or physical disorders with associated harmful behavior, and drug abuse or addiction.
snippet_highlighted_words: communicable diseases of public health significance, mental or physical disorders with associated harmful behavior, and drug abuse or addiction

text_blocks.snippet: 1. Communicable Diseases of Public Health Significance:

list.title: Tuberculosis:
list.snippet: Active, untreated tuberculosis (TB) is a significant concern and can lead to inadmissibility.

list.title: Syphilis:
list.snippet: Infectious syphilis can also be a disqualifying condition.

list.title: Other STIs:
list.snippet: Other sexually transmitted infections like gonorrhea and chancroid can also be problematic if not treated.

list.title: Leprosy:
list.snippet: Active leprosy (Hansen's disease) is another infectious disease that can lead to inadmissibility.

list.title: Novel or Pandemic Flu:
list.snippet: Any novel or pandemic influenza, as declared by the WHO, may also be a ground for inadmissibility.

text_blocks.snippet: 2. Mental or Physical Disorders with Associated Harmful Behavior:

list.snippet: This category is not simply about having a mental illness, but rather about whether that illness is associated with harmful behavior that could pose a threat to the applicant or others.
Examples include violent behavior, self-harm, or the inability to control one's actions due to a mental disorder.
Physical disorders that could render an individual unable to support themselves or that require extensive medical care may also be considered.
A history of drug abuse or addiction can be a factor in determining green card eligibility.
Active drug addiction is likely to be a disqualifying factor.
Even a history of drug abuse may require documentation of treatment or ongoing monitoring.
Failure to receive required vaccinations: Applicants must provide proof of certain required vaccinations.
Public Charge: If the applicant is deemed likely to become a public charge (relying on public assistance), this can also be a ground for inadmissibility.
The presence of a condition does not always automatically lead to denial. Waivers may be available in some cases.
The final decision rests with the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), which takes into account the specific circumstances of each case.
It's crucial for applicants to be forthcoming about their medical history and to seek legal counsel if they have any concerns about potential health-related issues.

text_blocks.snippet: For more specific information and guidance, it is recommended to consult with an immigration attorney or a medical professional specializing in immigration exams.
